title: What the Middle East conflict reveals about global tourism
gist: WEF argues the late-February 2026 Middle East conflict, which cancelled 23,000+ flights and crippled Dubai/Doha/Abu Dhabi hubs, exposed global tourism's dangerous dependence on a few Gulf transit corridors; rerouting merely transferred stress elsewhere. It proposes connectivity, governance and destination resilience and urges treating tourism as a strategic, infrastructure-like sector akin to energy and semiconductors.

insights.claim: When Middle East conflict escalated in late February 2026, more than 23,000 flights were cancelled within days and airports in Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi operated below normal capacity.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the 2026 aviation disruption hitting Gulf carriers and airports.
insights.quote: Within days, more than 23,000 flights had been cancelled
insights.locator: When conflict escalated across the Middle East

insights.claim: The 2026 geopolitical shock propagated rapidly from aviation to destinations, fuel markets and traveller confidence, ultimately hitting incomes of hotels, retailers, event organizers and small businesses far from the conflict zone.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Conflict risk in the Gulf transmits to travel-exposed earnings globally, not just regionally.
insights.locator: The events of 2026 demonstrated

insights.claim: Rerouting around contracted Gulf hubs was not a simple fix because aviation networks are constrained by bilateral air-service agreements, airport slots, aircraft range, overflight permissions and crew economics, so alternative capacity was partial, slow and more expensive.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Capacity substitution is sticky; disruptions to hubs imply prolonged fare/cost spikes rather than quick normalization.
insights.quote: When Gulf hubs contracted, rerouting was not a simple fix.
insights.locator: When Gulf hubs contracted

insights.claim: Longer reroutes during the 2026 disruption raised airline fuel and insurance costs, while air-cargo capacity fell as Middle Eastern carriers were affected.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Margin pressure for airlines and tighter air-freight capacity are second-order effects of Gulf disruption.
insights.quote: Longer routes also raised fuel and insurance costs
insights.locator: When Gulf hubs contracted

insights.claim: Displaced travel demand produces 'stress transfer' rather than resilience: demand shifts to other routes and destinations, some already struggling with congestion, housing pressure and community concerns.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Apparent beneficiaries of rerouted demand may face capacity and political backlash rather than clean upside.
insights.quote: moving pressure from one node to another is not the same as making the system more resilient
insights.locator: The result was stress transfer

insights.claim: UN Tourism recorded 95 million international arrivals to the Middle East in 2024, 32% above pre-pandemic levels.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Middle East tourism has outgrown pre-COVID levels sharply, raising exposure to regional conflict.
insights.quote: UN Tourism recorded 95 million international arrivals to the Middle East in 2024, 32% above pre-pandemic levels.
insights.locator: The Gulf: a destination that also moves the world

insights.claim: Dubai welcomed 19.5 million international overnight visitors in 2025 and its airport processed 101 million passengers in 2024, while Saudi Arabia's airports handled 128 million passengers.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Scale of Gulf aviation throughput underlines how much global traffic rides on a few nodes.
insights.locator: The Gulf: a destination that also moves the world

insights.claim: Doha's Hamad International Airport reported that 74% of its passengers were in transit, illustrating that Gulf airports function as switching stations for long-haul travel linking Europe with Asia, Africa and the Americas.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Transit-heavy hub models are highly exposed to corridor shutdowns since demand is not destination-anchored.
insights.quote: Hamad International Airport, for example, reported that 74% of its passengers were in transit.
insights.locator: The Gulf: a destination that also moves the world

insights.claim: Gulf hubs' location, airline networks and operating models make many long-haul city pairs economically viable, so their disruption breaks connectivity far beyond the region.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Hub disruption removes viable routes globally, affecting carriers and destinations such as Bali and Bangkok.
insights.quote: They are switching stations in the architecture of long-haul travel.
insights.locator: These hubs are not simply large regional airports

insights.claim: Investment is deepening hub concentration: Dubai's Al Maktoum International Airport is being developed for an eventual 260 million passengers a year and Riyadh's King Salman International Airport is designed for 120 million passengers by 2030.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Mega-hub capex increases systemic single-point-of-failure risk in global aviation.
insights.locator: Investment is deepening that concentration

insights.claim: After October 2023, tourist arrivals to Israel fell from around 300,000 in September to roughly 38,000 by November, per Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Active conflict can cut inbound tourism by ~87% within two months.
insights.locator: The relationship between conflict and tourism

insights.claim: In 2025 Canadian visits to the United States fell by roughly 25%, costing the US economy more than $8 billion in visitor spending, driven by diplomatic tensions and political rhetoric rather than a broad travel slowdown.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Political rhetoric alone can inflict measurable losses on US travel, hospitality and retail.
insights.quote: In 2025, Canadian visits to the United States fell by roughly 25%
insights.locator: But equally revealing disruptions can occur

insights.claim: Tourism Economics estimated the 2025 US inbound shortfall represented an opportunity cost of roughly $25 billion versus expected growth, even as worldwide 80 million more people travelled abroad.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The US lost share in a growing global travel market, a relative underperformance signal.
insights.locator: But equally revealing disruptions can occur

insights.claim: Because tourism reacts to physical danger, diplomatic tensions, visa restrictions and perception changes, it often registers shifts in confidence before they appear in other economic indicators.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Travel flow data can be used as a leading indicator of geopolitical and confidence shifts.
insights.quote: Tourism therefore often registers shifts in confidence before they appear in other economic indicators.
insights.locator: These episodes illustrate the conditions

insights.claim: Connectivity resilience requires diverse routing geographies, direct services, alternative hubs and multimodal options, with European rail investment cited as a source of redundancy and sustainability.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Points to policy support for alternative hubs, direct routes and rail as redundancy plays.
insights.locator: First is connectivity resilience

insights.claim: Governance resilience requires airlines, airports, tourism ministries, immigration authorities, insurers, payment providers, online platforms, hotels and local governments to share information and have tested mechanisms to reallocate capacity and support affected businesses.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Expect more public-private crisis coordination mechanisms involving travel platforms and insurers.
insights.locator: Second is governance resilience

insights.claim: Destination resilience means diversifying source markets and seasons, managing visitor flows, investing in shared infrastructure and strengthening small-business participation, while protecting perceptions of stability that can shift before physical conditions do.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Destinations dependent on single source markets or hubs carry concentration risk.
insights.quote: perceptions of stability, accessibility and welcome can change before physical conditions do
insights.locator: Third is destination resilience

insights.claim: Travel and tourism generated an estimated $11.6 trillion in global GDP and supported 357 million jobs in 2025, according to the World Travel & Tourism Council.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Sizes the economic base exposed to mobility shocks.
insights.locator: The disruption exposed more than an aviation crisis

insights.claim: The authors argue tourism should be reclassified as a strategic, infrastructure-like system, analogous to how energy gained strategic reserves after the 1970s oil shocks and semiconductors became central to industrial policy after supply-chain crises.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Strategic designation could bring state funding, redundancy mandates and industrial policy to aviation and tourism infrastructure.
insights.quote: After 2026, treating global tourism infrastructure as a strategic system is no longer a distant ambition. It is overdue.
insights.locator: A strategic sector overdue for strategic treatment

insights.claim: The lesson of 2026 is not to curb mobility or tourism growth but to build redundancy, coordination and local capacity so both can endure shocks.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Signals continued growth orientation with added resilience capex rather than demand restraint.
insights.quote: The practical lesson is not to reduce mobility or tourism growth.
